sections.title: Cost by Hiring Model: Freelancer, Agency, or In-House

inline: The second biggest driver is who does the work. The same build can cost three times more at an agency than at a freelance developer in a lower-cost region, but the agency includes project management, QA, and backup capacity that a solo freelancer does not.
For a deeper regional breakdown of freelance pricing in the US specifically, see our guide to

t: freelance ecommerce developer costs in the USA

inline: Agencies typically charge $75 to $200 per hour, or quote fixed-price projects from $15,000 upward. The premium buys project management, QA, post-launch support, and continuity if one developer leaves. For builds over $30,000 or any project with complex integrations, the agency premium is usually worth it.

A full-time ecommerce developer in the US costs $80,000 to $150,000 per year in salary, plus 20 to 35 percent in benefits, taxes, and equipment. Recruitment adds another $10,000 to $20,000 upfront. In-house makes sense only when you have a continuous pipeline of development work.

Best for well-defined builds with a clear scope document. You get a total number up front, but changes outside the scope become expensive change orders. Ask for a detailed scope document, not a one-line quote.

Best for ongoing, exploratory, or open-ended work. You pay for time actually spent, which is fair for maintenance or bug fixing but risky for a full build with no defined endpoint. Always ask for a weekly timesheet and a cap.

sections.title: What Drives Ecommerce Developer Cost Up or Down

inline: Two projects with the same headline scope can come in at wildly different prices. The difference is almost always in the details below.

items: Any deviation from the platform's default checkout multiplies testing and QA time.
Each integration (ERP, CRM, PIM, accounting, shipping, loyalty) adds development and testing time.
Moving products, customers, and orders from a legacy platform is error-prone and needs careful validation.
Localization adds significant complexity to cart, tax, and content.
A custom design system costs far more than an adapted theme.
High-traffic stores need optimization work that simple builds skip.

b: Reusing an existing design or brand.

Launch a lean core store and add features after launch.

sections.title: How to Budget: A Simple Worksheet

inline: Use the following approach to turn the ranges above into a realistic budget number for your project.
Pick the row in the project-type table that matches your scope. Add 15 percent as a contingency for scope changes. This is your build budget.

Add hosting, platform subscriptions, plugin licenses, and maintenance for the first year. For a small WooCommerce store, expect an additional $1,000 to $3,000. For Shopify, $500 to $2,000. For custom builds, $5,000 to $30,000.
Reserve 5 to 10 percent of the build cost for post-launch fixes, unexpected plugin needs, and marketing setup. Most launches reveal something that needs fixing in the first 30 days.

faqs.q: How much does an ecommerce website developer cost per hour?
a: Rates range from about $20 per hour for junior developers in lower-cost regions to $200 or more per hour for senior agency developers in the US. The median for a mid-level ecommerce developer in the US is roughly $75 to $120 per hour.

faqs.q: Is $5,000 enough to build an ecommerce website?
a: Yes, if you are building a template-based store with a clear scope and minimal custom work. $5,000 typically covers a Shopify or WooCommerce theme setup, product upload, and basic apps. Custom checkouts or multiple integrations will push past that budget.

faqs.q: Why is a custom ecommerce build so much more expensive?
a: Custom builds require original design, custom checkout logic, third-party integrations, and extensive QA that template builds skip. Each of those phases adds development and testing hours, which multiply quickly as scope grows.

faqs.q: Should I hire a freelancer or an agency to save money?
a: A freelancer is usually 30 to 60 percent cheaper than an agency for the same scope. The trade-off is that you manage the project, and you carry the risk if the freelancer disappears or delivers late. For projects over $30,000, the agency premium usually pays for itself in delivery reliability.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay the full amount upfront?
a: No. Standard practice is a deposit of 25 to 50 percent, with the rest tied to milestones and final delivery. Be cautious of any developer who requests full payment upfront, or who refuses to define milestones in writing. See
